captions: Hello, and welcome to Camday English, Stage 9. In this lesson: The printing press.
Read an explanatory text and identify causes and effects.
Here are some new words. Revolution. A very big change in the way things are done. Spread.
Move to cover a larger area or more people. Literacy. The ability to read and write.
And some more words. Access. The ability to get or use something. Impact. A strong effect. Widespread.
Happening in many places or among many people.
Time for a question. The video will stop. Which word means: a very big change in the way things are done?
Now some grammar: Cause and effect language.
Use due to or because of with a noun; as a result or consequently with a clause; and led to or resulted in with a noun,
to explain causes and effects. For example: Books became cheaper due to printing.
For example: As a result, more people learned to read. For example: Printing led to a rise in literacy.
Now listen, and read along. How the printing press changed the world.
Before the fifteenth century, every book in Europe had to be copied by hand.
A single book could take months to produce, so books were rare and expensive,
and only a small number of people could read.
In around 1440, Johannes Gutenberg developed a printing press that used movable metal letters.
A page could be arranged, inked and pressed onto paper again and again.
As a result, books could be produced hundreds of times faster than before.
The impact was enormous.
Because of cheaper books, more people had access to knowledge, and literacy became more widespread.
New ideas in science, religion and politics spread quickly across countries.
Some historians argue that the printing press led to some of the greatest changes in European history.
In many ways, it was the information revolution of its time – much like the internet today.
Another question. The video will stop. How were books made before the fifteenth century?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like revolution, spread, literacy.
You practised cause and effect language. And you read How the printing press changed the world.
Now try the practice questions. See you next time!

captions: Hello, and welcome to Camday English, Stage 9. In this lesson: From verbs to nouns.
Use nominalisation to write in a more academic style.
Here are some new words. Nominalisation. Turning a verb or adjective into a noun. Academic.
Used in schools, universities and serious study. Vaccination.
Giving someone a vaccine to protect them from disease.
And some more words. Development. The process of growing or changing. Reduction.
The act of making something smaller. Discovery. Finding something for the first time.
Time for a question. The video will stop. Which word means: turning a verb or adjective into a noun?
Now some grammar: Nominalisation.
Academic writing often uses nouns instead of verbs: discover becomes discovery, reduce becomes reduction,
develop becomes development, improve becomes improvement. This makes writing more formal and compact.
For example: Scientists discovered penicillin, which saved millions,
becomes: The discovery of penicillin saved millions.
Now listen, and read along. The idea of vaccination.
The development of vaccination is often described as one of the greatest achievements in medicine. In 1796,
the English doctor Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had caught a mild disease called cowpox rarely caught smallpox,
a far more dangerous illness.
His observation led to an experiment: he gave a boy material from a
cowpox sore and later showed that the boy was protected from smallpox.
The discovery that the body could be trained to fight disease changed medicine forever.
Over the following two centuries,
the introduction of vaccines for diseases such as polio and measles led to a dramatic reduction in illness and death.
In 1980, after a global vaccination programme,
smallpox was declared eradicated – the first human disease to be completely removed from the world.
Another question. The video will stop. Who was Edward Jenner?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like nominalisation, academic, vaccination.
You practised nominalisation. And you read The idea of vaccination. Now try the practice questions.
See you next time!
